findings.intent: localeCovered() is documented as 'Whether a provider covers a requested locale'; Doc 10 line 182 lists 'language quality' as a routing factor.
findings.reality: localeCovered() only sets a ranking flag. A provider declaring ['sw'] is still eligible for an 'en-KE' request and is selected when it is the only candidate - the reason string even reports 'capabilities do not include the requested locale' while still selecting it. The Tier 0 provider treats the same condition as a hard filter (tier-zero.ts:115-128).
findings.evidence: policy.ts:200 (localeMatch) and 205-206 (sort key only); no 'locale' member exists in the PolicyRejection.rule union (policy.ts:64). tier-zero.ts:124-127 filters strictly.
findings.failure_mode: The learner can be routed to a provider that does not serve their language, while the offline tier refuses the same mismatch - the two halves of the ladder disagree about what a locale mismatch means.
findings.fix: Add 'locale' to PolicyRejection.rule and make coverage an eligibility rule (or document explicitly that coverage is advisory and align Tier 0 with it).

findings.title: The local-echo input-token estimate ignores the request context, under-charging the ledger
findings.intent: 'Rough token estimate. Deterministic and dependency-free.'
findings.reality: estimateTokens(req.prompt) counts only the prompt; req.context (grounded sources) and req.system are excluded, so the tokens actually sent are not the tokens charged.
findings.evidence: local-echo.ts:77-81 (the digest and the usage both use req.prompt only); the adapter also never reads req.context when composing its answer.
findings.failure_mode: The ledger under-counts the local tier's cost, and the offline 'free' path silently consumes provider capacity without being accounted for.
findings.fix: Estimate over prompt + system + context, or state that the local tier is uncharged by design.

findings.title: Redaction is string-only and is skipped on some of the same package's error paths
findings.intent: 'Everything that is written into a reason string goes through here first' and 'The package never logs a credential'.
findings.reality: redactSecret can only mask a string; it cannot traverse a nested object, an array, a header map or a stack. The gateway applies it to attempt reasons and error messages only - not to result.text (the provider's answer, which is delivered verbatim to the learner) and not to meta.policyReason (F3-10). conformance.ts:58-60 defines its own describeError with no redaction at all.
findings.evidence: redact.ts:35-41 (string in, string out); gateway.ts:202 (redactSecret(reason)) vs gateway.ts:508 (policyReason assigned raw); conformance.ts:58-60 `function describeError(err) { return err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err); }` with no redactSecret import.
findings.failure_mode: A provider that echoes a credential in its answer text delivers it to the learner and stores it in the result; the conformance report can echo a raw provider message into a report file.
findings.fix: Redact the provider answer before delivery (or make redaction a structured, recursive function), and use the redacting describeError in conformance.ts.

findings.title: Dead options and exports: refuseOverBudget, timeoutMs, GatewayOptions.policyEngine, tryProjectEgressPayload
findings.intent: Every exported surface is a promise that something uses it.
findings.reality: MockAdapterOptions.refuseOverBudget is implemented but no test ever sets it (the budget-refusal test uses failWith with a BudgetExceededError instead). QwenAdapterOptions.timeoutMs is never set by any caller so the timeout is always 30s. GatewayOptions.policyEngine is never set by any caller. tryProjectEgressPayload and NEVER_EGRESS_DATA_CLASSES are public exports with no production consumer.
findings.evidence: rg 'refuseOverBudget' -> support.ts:137 and 171 only. rg 'timeoutMs' -> qwen-adapter.ts:84,138,177,227 only. rg 'policyEngine:' -> gateway.ts:90 (the interface member) only. rg 'tryProjectEgressPayload' -> egress.ts:179,184 and egress.test.ts only. rg 'NEVER_EGRESS_DATA_CLASSES' -> egress.ts:51,161 only.
findings.failure_mode: The public surface advertises capabilities that no consumer exercises (an untested timeout knob, an untested policy-engine injection, a non-throwing egress helper); reviewers and callers cannot tell which knobs are real.
findings.fix: Delete the unused knobs or add the tests that exercise them; keep the public surface honest.

findings.title: Test suite does not cover several adversarial/contract-risk cases (negative money at append, unicode-homoglyph/ZWSP field evasions beyond normalization assumptions, sponsor-report key drift failures)
findings.intent: Tests should prevent regressions in stated invariants: no invalid money states, robust PII boundary under adversarial naming/values, and loud failure on reporting contract drift.
findings.reality: Existing tests are meaningful for basic tamper/PII/correction/reproducibility, but gaps remain: no test asserts rejection of negative money-key values at append (270-281 only checks non-integer float); no explicit ZWSP/unicode-variant forbidden field test; no tests proving sponsor report behavior when producer keys differ (current behavior is silent defaults, untested as risk); no concurrency/fork tests (in-memory design makes this N/A but relevant if persisted).
findings.evidence: ledger-store.test.ts:270-281; pii-guard.test.ts lacks ZWSP example despite normalize stripping non-alnum (pii-guard.ts:140-142 likely handles it, but unproven by test); sponsor-report.test.ts fixtures always use canonical keys. No tests for `valueScan:'off'` migration path except behavior implied? ledger-store.test.ts:303-337 covers valueScan off/on interplay.
findings.failure_mode: Regressions in uncovered edge cases (e.g. allowing negative money, silent metric corruption on schema drift) may ship undetected, giving false confidence from green tests.
findings.fix: Add negative tests for negative money-key append rejection, unicode confusable/ZWSP forbidden field names, explicit report behavior on missing/renamed keys (assert anomaly/failure once implemented), and concurrency/transaction tests if/when storage becomes durable.

findings.title: PII guard value scanning cannot detect names/free-text PII under innocuous keys or obfuscated/non-pattern values
findings.intent: Public ledger/sponsor artefacts must never contain personal data; the guard is a defense-in-depth boundary but claims/expectations may exceed its provable coverage.
findings.reality: Field-name defense is strong (normalized recursive). Value defense scans only string values for email (V1), long digit runs (V2), and phone-shaped patterns starting with '+' or '0' (V3), with exemptions (205-276). It does not detect personal names, addresses, prose identifiers, or PII in non-matching formats/encodings under unknown keys. Numeric values are never scanned.
findings.evidence: pii-guard.ts:26-35 documents limits; 205-210 published rules V1-V3 only; 247-276 string-only checks. Allowed-field test includes `note: 'quarterly allocation'` (ledger-store.test.ts:185-195) showing free text is permitted if no pattern match; adversarial personal names in innocuous keys would pass if not matching V1-V3.
findings.failure_mode: Personal data that is not email/phone/digit-shaped (e.g. learner name, location narrative) can be appended and published if placed under a non-forbidden key, violating the no-PII boundary despite guard/self-scan passing.
findings.fix: Treat guard as necessary-but-not-sufficient: enforce strict payload schemas/allowlists per entry type, prohibit arbitrary free-text fields in public payloads, and add policy/review/static checks for non-pattern PII. Consider stronger classifiers only with explicit false-positive handling.

findings.title: Private-store separation and privacy are enforced by in-memory convention/interface, not durable isolation/encryption controls
findings.intent: Private operational data (identity, consent, safeguarding, transcripts) must be stored separately from the public ledger with strong isolation and minimization guarantees.
findings.reality: `createPrivateStore` is an in-memory Map with no persistence path, no encryption-at-rest, no key protection, and no access control boundary beyond module/API convention (149-192). Redaction produces aggregates but does not provide cryptographic separation from source records in-process.
findings.evidence: private-store.ts:28-33 explicitly states in-memory by design and defers persistence/retention/wipe; 149-191 store/copy behavior only. No filesystem, crypto, or permission primitives. Hunt (h) asks where it writes/encrypted/protected — implementation writes nowhere and is plaintext in memory.
findings.failure_mode: A service embedding this store without additional controls would have no durable private-store security properties (encryption, tenancy isolation, retention enforcement) from this package; memory disclosure/process dumps could expose raw records.
findings.fix: Document non-goals clearly at API boundary and implement/require a hardened persistence adapter in the owning service (encrypted storage, access control, retention/wipe, audit) before handling real private data.

findings.title: Sponsor report does not fail when ledger chain is broken; it publishes a report with chainOk=false
findings.intent: Sponsor-facing evidence should be trustworthy; a broken/tampered ledger chain undermines the validity of derived financial and impact claims.
findings.reality: `buildSponsorReport` records verification result (`verification = ledger.verify()`) into `report.ledger.chainOk/brokenAtSeq/chainDetail` but continues computing and returning the full report (255-327). It does not throw or gate publication on integrity.
findings.evidence: sponsor-report.ts:255,263-269 include chain status fields; no conditional abort. Caller must inspect `ledger.chainOk` themselves.
findings.failure_mode: Consumers may overlook `chainOk=false` and rely on funding/usage aggregates computed from untrusted/tampered source state, weakening audit guarantees.
findings.fix: Provide a strict mode that throws on broken chain (using `assertChainIntact`) or clearly separate 'unverified draft' outputs; default sponsor-facing publication paths should refuse to emit on integrity failure.

findings.title: The hosted settings server is unauthenticated and internet-reachable, disclosing the API-key names and lengths and absolute filesystem paths
findings.intent: serve.ts: hosted mode 'is a read-only demonstration, never a remote settings editor'.
findings.reality: authorizePeer() returns allowed for EVERY peer when hosted=true, and the host binds 0.0.0.0. GET /api/settings returns the masked settings plus describeApiKeys(), which reports the name, the 'set' boolean and the LENGTH of every provider key; /api/health returns the absolute path of the settings file and the Node version. There is no authentication, no token and no rate limit.
findings.evidence: serve.ts:92-99 `if (hosted) return { allowed: true };`  /  :194 `const host = flagString(args,'host') ?? (hosted ? '0.0.0.0' : loaded.settings.server.host);`  /  :122 `setByPath(masked, 'providers.apiKeys', describeApiKeys(settings));`  /  settings-store.ts:402-410 describeApiKeys returns { set, length }.
findings.failure_mode: Key names and exact key lengths are public, which materially narrows brute force and tells an attacker exactly which provider is configured; the deployment's filesystem layout and runtime version are disclosed.
findings.fix: Require an auth token for hosted mode, drop key lengths from describeApiKeys, and stop returning absolute paths over HTTP.

findings.title: The kill switch is process-local: a restart resurrects a provider killed for a safety, residency or licence failure
findings.intent: kill-switch.ts: 'a killed provider is a governance decision (safety incident, data-residency breach, licence problem). It takes effect immediately and outranks every routing preference.'
findings.reality: The killed set is a `new Map<string, string>()` in memory. It is not persisted, not shared between instances and not reconstructed at startup, so the governance decision evaporates on restart. The KillSwitch interface also exposes revive() with no actor, no authorisation and no second-person rule.
findings.evidence: kill-switch.ts:31 `const killed = new Map<string, string>();` and :39-41 revive() deletes unconditionally  /  gateway.ts:248 checks killSwitch.isKilled() per request only.
findings.failure_mode: A provider is killed after a data-residency breach. The service is restarted (deploy, crash, machine reboot) and the provider is routed to again with no record that it was ever killed — and the kill trail itself is lost with it.
findings.fix: Persist the kill list (and its reason and timestamp) in the durable store, load it at startup, and require an authorised actor + reason for both kill and revive.

findings.title: CI does not implement the 9.2 GL-01..GL-08 pipeline the Phase 0 work item promises
findings.intent: 09 12.2 work item: 'the CI pipeline with the GL-01…GL-08 stages (9.2)'; 9.2 defines 9 stages (intake, branch+build, static analysis, independent review, rework, loop testing, correction, resolution, package/sign/deploy).
findings.reality: ci.yml has 5 jobs (typecheck, test, secrets, sbom, verify); no SAST/DAST, licence audit, ledger-compatibility, rollback-test or independent-review stage.
findings.evidence: ci.yml jobs at lines 24-150; no job named for GL-01..GL-08; the only scan is npm run secrets:scan.
findings.failure_mode: The Phase 0 'CI with the GL-01…GL-08 stages' promise is narrowed to a build/test/scan pipeline without the narrowing being recorded; 'CI green' covers far less than the spec's release gate.
findings.fix: Either add the missing stages or record the Slice 0 narrowing in the session log/ADR and correct the Phase 0 work-item claim.

findings.title: The gateway can be constructed with a policy engine that holds a different breaker and kill switch than the gateway's own
findings.intent: GatewayOptions lets a deployment inject a policy engine; the gateway and the engine are supposed to share one breaker and one kill switch.
findings.reality: opts.policyEngine is used verbatim, while the gateway's own breaker/killSwitch (opts.breaker/opts.killSwitch or fresh instances) are used for its per-candidate checks. If the injected engine was built with different breaker/killSwitch instances, the decision and the execution disagree about which providers are tripped or killed. No test covers this configuration.
findings.evidence: gateway.ts:155-169 (three independent sources of breaker/killSwitch) and gateway.ts:248-260 (the gateway's own checks) vs policy.ts:155-175 (the engine's checks). rg 'policyEngine:' -> gateway.ts:90 only: the option is never exercised.
findings.failure_mode: A deployment that injects a policy engine with its own breaker silently gets two independent breaker states, so a provider can be routed by the engine and skipped by the gateway (or the reverse).
findings.fix: Derive the gateway's breaker/killSwitch from the injected engine, or reject the combination; add a test.

findings.title: Provider statusText is returned to the audit trail without redaction
findings.intent: redact.ts: everything written into a reason string goes through redactSecret first.
findings.reality: readErrorDetail redacts the JSON error.message, but when the body is not JSON it returns response.statusText raw. statusText is provider-controlled and lands in the gateway attempt trail.
findings.evidence: qwen-adapter.ts:300-316: `return response.statusText || 'no detail was returned';` - no redactSecret call on that path.
findings.failure_mode: A provider echoing a key in its status line lands unredacted in the audit trail.
findings.fix: Apply redactSecret to the statusText fallback.

findings.title: Double-count detection for semantically duplicated funding/allocation records is absent; engine trusts ledger entries as unique facts
findings.intent: The 60% engine must not misstate compliance due to double-counting (build log concern: same amount recorded as both allocation and device purchase or otherwise duplicated).
findings.reality: Engine classifies by `entry.type` and sums amounts: funding types add to base, `reinvestment_allocation` adds to allocated; other types excluded (141-184). It does not detect duplicate economic events recorded as multiple entries, cross-references, idempotency keys, or semantic overlap between allocation and purchase events (purchase types not modeled here).
findings.evidence: reinvestment.ts:141-184 has no dedupe/idempotency logic; exclusions only record reasons like outside period or not funding type. Correctly avoids counting the same entry as both base and allocation, but cannot catch duplicated entries representing same underlying transaction.
findings.failure_mode: Duplicated or semantically overlapping entries can inflate eligible base or allocated totals, causing incorrect compliance outcomes and audit discrepancies despite deterministic arithmetic.
findings.fix: Require/validate idempotency or source-reference fields per economic event, detect duplicates (by ref/hash/business key) during computation, and surface suspected double-counts as exclusions/anomalies requiring reconciliation.

findings.title: projectGroundedContext's locator check misses drive-relative and scheme-only path forms
findings.intent: egress.ts: 'The locator is a CONTENT identifier (curriculum:algebra/linear-eq), never a filesystem path and never a URL.'
findings.reality: locatorIsUnsafe rejects `^[A-Za-z]:[\\/]` (drive + separator), a leading '/' or '\\', any '://', a leading 'file:' and control characters. It does NOT reject the drive-RELATIVE form 'C:secrets' (no separator after the colon), nor a scheme-only URL such as 'https:example.com/x' (single colon, no '//'), nor a UNC-style share locator written with a non-leading separator. The projector therefore still emits a locator that names the build machine's filesystem.
findings.evidence: egress.ts:208-220 `if (/^[A-Za-z]:[\\/]/.test(locator)) return true; if (locator.startsWith('/') || locator.startsWith('\\')) return true; if (locator.includes('://')) return true; if (/^file:/i.test(locator)) return true;`
findings.failure_mode: A build-machine path fragment naming a drive-relative user directory, or an internal scheme-qualified host, is transmitted to the third-party provider in every grounded message, disclosing the operator's directory layout.
findings.fix: Use a positive allowlist for locator shapes (e.g. only `scheme:` tokens from a known set, no separators) instead of a blocklist of path prefixes.

findings.title: The secrets scanner never scans git history and skips the artifacts directory, and the published checksum manifest carries a digest of the plaintext API-key file
findings.intent: secrets-scan.mjs header: 'Scans the tree that a commit would publish for likely secrets.'
findings.reality: publishedFiles() uses `git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard`, which lists the current index and working tree only — history is never inspected, so a deleted-but-committed secret is never found. SKIP_DIRECTORIES excludes 'artifacts', so the published attestation, SBOM, verify report and checksum manifest are never scanned. Separately, tools/checksums.mjs walks the whole 'settings' directory, so artifacts/checksums.sha256 (a TRACKED, published file) contains the SHA-256 of settings/settings.local.json — the plaintext API-key file.
findings.evidence: secrets-scan.mjs:121-134 git ls-files only  /  :31-40 SKIP_DIRECTORIES includes 'artifacts'  /  checksums.mjs:54 INCLUDE_ROOTS includes 'settings' and :91-100 walks it — the live artifacts/checksums.sha256 contains the line for settings/settings.local.json.
findings.failure_mode: A leaked key is committed, deleted in a later commit, and the scanner reports PASS because history is out of scope. Separately, the published manifest is an offline oracle for the contents of the secret file: anyone who can guess the key can confirm it by hashing candidate files.
findings.fix: Scan git history (git rev-list --objects --all | git cat-file) or document the exclusion; do not exclude the artifacts directory; and exclude settings/*.local.json from the checksum manifest (and from the attestation's subject list).

findings.title: The enrolmentMethod attribute is written and never read
findings.intent: The path taken is recorded so it can be audited.
findings.reality: attributes['enrolmentMethod'] is written on the principal but read nowhere in the tree. The audit trail does record the path (EnrolmentAuditEvent.method), so the attribute is a second, dead copy of it.
findings.evidence: grep -rn 'enrolmentMethod' -> enrolment.ts:359 (write) only; the policy engine reads linkedLearnerIds and guardianConsent (policy.ts:159, :170) but not enrolmentMethod
findings.failure_mode: Dead state on the principal invites a future reader to trust an attribute that nothing maintains.
findings.fix: Either remove the attribute or make a consumer of it. The audit trail is already the record of truth.

findings.title: P0-2's evidence is a string-contains check that cannot detect a missing owner or an 'unassigned' status
findings.intent: 09 12.2 exit criterion 2: 'Every ADR in 11 shows a named Owner and a recorded Status; none reads unassigned.'
findings.reality: The gate only checks that the README contains three literal strings.
findings.evidence: exit-criteria.json P0-2 evidence contains ['| ADR | Title | Status | Owner |','ADR-0016','Accepted']; the exit-criteria gate's file check (exit-criteria-gate.ts:223-245) does a substring match and never parses the table, so a row with Owner '—' or Status 'unassigned' would still pass.
findings.failure_mode: The criterion can be reported met while an ADR row is unassigned; the check proves the register exists, not that the register satisfies the criterion.
findings.fix: Parse docs/adr/README.md in the gate and assert every ADR row has a non-empty owner and a status in {Accepted, Proposed, Superseded}.

findings.title: The ARC-I4 uncertainty note is unreachable: no adapter in the package reports confidence
findings.intent: 'uncertainty_note is present whenever the provider reports confidence below the routing threshold (ARC-I4).'
findings.reality: The branch depends on result.confidence. The Qwen adapter (qwen-adapter.ts:270-277), local-echo (local-echo.ts:90-98) and tier-zero (tier-zero.ts:141-148) all return CompletionResult objects with no confidence field, so confidence is always undefined and uncertainty_note is always null.
findings.evidence: rg 'confidence' across packages/onekey/src -> only gateway.ts (the read + the branch) and the DEFAULT_CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD import. No adapter sets it.
findings.failure_mode: The uncertainty marker is dead code in production; a low-confidence answer is delivered with no uncertainty note and no test can ever reach the branch.
findings.fix: Map a provider confidence field in the adapters, or drop the ARC-I4 claim and the branch.

findings.title: `all()` exposes live mutable entry objects, permitting in-process mutation/deletion outside append-only API semantics
findings.intent: Append-only means existing entries cannot be updated or deleted through any public API; corrections must be compensating entries.
findings.reality: While there is no `update`/`delete` method, `all()` intentionally returns the live internal array and live entry objects (256-269). Callers can mutate payload/hash/link fields or splice entries, breaking the chain. `exportPublic()` is the safe copy path (310-319). README documents this as tamper-evidence/testability choice.
findings.evidence: ledger-store.ts:256 comment explicitly states live array returned; tests mutate via `store.all()` to prove tamper detection (ledger-store.test.ts:78-86,90-104,109-115). No defensive copies/freeze on `all()`.
findings.failure_mode: Accidental or malicious in-process code holding a reference from `all()` can corrupt chain state without going through append/correction discipline; integrity becomes dependent on caller discipline despite append-only narrative.
findings.fix: Return deep-frozen snapshots from `all()` and keep a separate privileged internal accessor for auditor/tamper-test tooling, or rename/document `all()` as unsafe/internal and make safe copy the default.

findings.title: The half-open circuit does not admit exactly one probe, and the promotion happens on read
findings.intent: circuit-breaker.ts: 'The cooldown elapsed: allow exactly one probe (half-open).' Doc 09 line 833: 'closed -> open -> half-open'.
findings.reality: state() mutates the entry on every read (open -> half_open) and nothing tracks probe exclusivity: once half_open, every concurrent request passes the gateway's `breaker.state(id) === 'open'` check and calls the provider. There is no in-flight probe latch.
findings.evidence: circuit-breaker.ts:75-79 (read promotes); gateway.ts:257-260 (the only gate is `state(...) === 'open'`). PROBE 11 (executed) confirmed the read-promotes behaviour; the entry shape {state, consecutiveFailures, openedAt, lastDetail} shows exclusivity is unrepresentable.
findings.failure_mode: After a cooldown, a burst of concurrent requests all probe the failing provider, re-triggering the failure storm the breaker was opened to stop.
findings.fix: Add an explicit probe latch (a boolean or an in-flight counter) so only one request may probe while half_open.

findings.title: The failover drill accepts an injected gateway while claiming 'The drill is offline'
findings.intent: failover.ts: 'The drill is offline: no key, no network, no hosted provider.'
findings.reality: FailoverDrillOptions.gateway lets a deployment inject its own gateway, which may contain live providers; the drill would then make real network calls and spend real credit while still being presented as the offline drill.
findings.evidence: failover.ts:55-58 ('A drill gateway is built when omitted'); failover.ts:20-27 ('The drill is offline: no key, no network, no hosted provider').
findings.failure_mode: A 'documented failover test' could be run against a live registry and produce a report indistinguishable from the offline one, while spending sponsor credit.
findings.fix: Assert that an injected gateway contains no non-local providers, or mark the report as live when an injected gateway is used.

findings.title: The per-request attempt trail is never evicted
findings.intent: attemptsFor(requestId) is a live audit surface for a long-running service.
findings.reality: attemptsByRequest is a Map that is written on every complete() and never pruned. There is no TTL, no size bound and no removal.
findings.evidence: gateway.ts:170 `const attemptsByRequest = new Map<string, GatewayAttempt[]>();`, gateway.ts:190 `attemptsByRequest.set(ctx.requestId, attempts);` - no delete anywhere in the file. PROBE 19 (executed): the trail for request 'r0' is still retrievable after 5 later requests.
findings.failure_mode: Unbounded memory growth in a long-running gateway: one retained array per request id, forever.
findings.fix: Bound the map (LRU) or move the trail to an external audit sink.

findings.title: The adapter has no retry, yet its 429 message advertises a retry-after hint that is never acted on
findings.intent: The error text says 'retry after 30s', implying the adapter honours the hint.
findings.reality: There is no retry loop anywhere in the adapter; the 429 is thrown immediately. The hint is informational only, and the gateway's response to it is to trip the circuit (F3-13).
findings.evidence: qwen-adapter.ts:242-249 builds the hint; rg 'retry' in qwen-adapter.ts returns only that message and the test that asserts it (qwen-adapter.test.ts:156-176).
findings.failure_mode: The log tells an operator the call will be retried after 30s when it will not be, and the provider is removed from routing instead.
findings.fix: Either implement the retry (honouring retry-after) or reword the message so it does not promise behaviour that does not exist.

findings.title: Deployment story in the docs is incomplete: env vars, PORT, health check and rollback are undocumented in the README
findings.intent: 09 9.4/9.7: the deployment allocation, health check and tested rollback are part of the release record; the README Deployment section is the owner-facing deployment story.
findings.reality: render.yaml carries NODE_VERSION, EDUGENESIS_HOSTED, Render-supplied PORT, healthCheckPath /api/health and autoDeployTrigger checksPass; the README Deployment section mentions none of the env vars, the port contract, the health path or rollback.
findings.evidence: render.yaml:32-40 startCommand/healthCheckPath/envVars; README.md:111-126 discusses the free tier, --hosted and 403 writes only; 9.7 requires a rollback plan tested before every rollout and no rollback procedure appears in README or render.yaml.
findings.failure_mode: An owner deploying from the README alone cannot know the health-check path or how to roll back; the deployment story is incomplete.
findings.fix: Document the env vars, the Render-supplied PORT, the /api/health check and the rollback procedure (Render rollback / previous successful deploy) in the README Deployment section.

findings.title: The emitted risk tier is hardcoded to 1 regardless of the request's safety tier
findings.intent: Doc 09 line 1044 (R16-04) requires pre-delivery risk tiering; ARC-I2 validates risk_tier; ARC-I3 requires source lineage at risk tier 2 and above.
findings.reality: buildEmission sets risk_tier: 1 for every request, and reading_level: {band:'unspecified'}, while req.safetyTier may be 'critical'. The comment 'THREE THINGS ARE COMPUTED, NEVER HARDCODED' lists three other fields, but the risk tier is a hardcoded constant right next to them.
findings.evidence: gateway.ts:575 `risk_tier: 1,` and gateway.ts:577 `reading_level: { band: 'unspecified' },`. accessibility/src/arc-invariants.ts:122-148 validates risk_tier only for range and for lineage presence at tier >= 2, so a constant 1 always satisfies the validator.
findings.failure_mode: A critical-safety-tier answer is emitted as the lowest risk tier, so the ARC lineage requirement for tier 2+ never triggers and downstream risk-based routing cannot see the real tier.
findings.fix: Derive risk_tier from req.safetyTier and validate the mapping against Doc 6 §3.1.

findings.title: A guardian consent token cannot be revoked before it expires
findings.intent: The file's own rule 2: a token is bound to one learner, expires, and is single-use.
findings.reality: There is no revoke path. The token lives for its 24-hour TTL unless it is used or expires, and the only way to neutralise it early is to let it be used.
findings.evidence: packages/identity/src/enrolment.ts:187-198 — the EnrolmentService interface exposes issue, enrol, passkey, auditTrail and isProvisional; no revoke
findings.failure_mode: A token captured in transit stays usable for up to a day after a guardian changes their mind.
findings.fix: Add revokeGuardianConsentToken and treat a revoked token id as spent.

findings.title: latencyMs is hardcoded to 0 in the network adapter
findings.intent: CompletionResult.latencyMs is 'Provider-reported latency in ms'; Doc 09 line 1320 lists 'model latency' as a monitored metric.
findings.reality: The Qwen adapter always returns latencyMs: 0 regardless of the real round-trip time.
findings.evidence: qwen-adapter.ts:276 `latencyMs: 0,` inside the returned CompletionResult; no timing variable exists in complete().
findings.failure_mode: The 'model latency' metric and any latency SLO computed from CompletionResult read a constant zero, hiding real provider latency regressions.
findings.fix: Measure the elapsed time around the fetch and report it.

findings.title: The registry snapshots capabilities at registration and the policy engine enforces the stale snapshot
findings.intent: 'Capabilities are snapshotted at registration so the registry stays inspectable even if an adapter is mid-restart.'
findings.reality: The safety-tier rule (policy.ts:144) and the data-class rule use entry.capabilities (the snapshot) while effectiveMaxDataClass additionally consults the live adapter.maxDataClass. A provider whose clearance is narrowed at runtime keeps the old clearedSafetyTiers for routing.
findings.evidence: registry.ts:63-65 `const capabilities = adapter.capabilities();`; policy.ts:144 `entry.capabilities.clearedSafetyTiers.includes(req.safetyTier)`; policy.ts:96-100 reads the live adapter only for maxDataClass.
findings.failure_mode: A provider whose clearance is revoked mid-flight remains eligible for the safety tier it was cleared for, and the kill switch is the only remaining control - which is per-process (F3-11).
findings.fix: Re-read capabilities for the hard rules, or re-snapshot the entry when the adapter's capabilities change.

findings.title: Payload timestamps accepted as any parseable date string, not strictly normalized ISO-8601; canonical preimage hashes the provided string form
findings.intent: Ledger entries should carry unambiguous, reproducible timestamps; canonicalization should prevent representational ambiguity in audited fields.
findings.reality: `assertTimestamp` only checks non-empty and `Date.parse(at)` parseability (200-207), accepting many non-ISO forms (e.g. locale-dependent or variant formats that `Date.parse` accepts). The stored/hashed `at` is the original string (235-251), not a normalized ISO form.
findings.evidence: ledger-store.ts:200-207 uses `Date.parse`; 235 sets `const timestamp = at ?? now()` and passes into preimage. Different string representations of the same instant would hash differently and both be accepted if parseable.
findings.failure_mode: Inconsistent timestamp encodings reduce interoperability and can complicate reproducible comparisons/audits; while not a hash collision, it permits ambiguous temporal representations in the public chain.
findings.fix: Require strict ISO-8601 format (and optionally normalize to `toISOString()` for generated/accepted values) before hashing/storing.

findings.title: 60% reinvestment excludes out-of-period allocations from compliance math, which can misstate compliance for period funding
findings.intent: Compliance should reflect whether reinvestment obligations for the eligible base in the period are met, with auditable inclusion/exclusion rules.
findings.reality: Entries outside the period (before or after) are excluded entirely before classification (124-136), including `reinvestment_allocation` entries (138-177). Thus an allocation that occurs after `period.to` but funds the same period's obligation is not counted, and the report can mark the period non-compliant even if sufficient reinvestment was later recorded.
findings.evidence: reinvestment.ts:124-136 exclude by timestamp for all entry types; 154-177 only in-period allocations contribute to `allocatedByCategory`. reinvestment.test.ts fixture includes seq 8 allocation after period excluded (47,84-85). No linkage field (e.g. obligation period) is considered.
findings.failure_mode: Period-bounded compliance results depend on allocation timing rather than obligation fulfillment, producing false negatives/positives relative to business intent unless periods and posting rules are perfectly aligned.
findings.fix: Define and implement allocation attribution explicitly (e.g. allocation period/obligation reference fields) or compute compliance over funding period with allocation matching rules; document current timestamp-only semantics prominently in report output.

surface_summaries.summary: Solo's own first-hand review of the live tree, independent of the three swarm surfaces, and every finding re-verified against the code rather than accepted from a report. The dominant theme: the slice is a LIBRARY plus a GATE SUITE. It contains no learner runtime, no durable store and no audit trail that outlives the process, and the documentation claimed otherwise in three places (an ADR, a package README and the Render Blueprint). The crypto and the core invariants are genuinely sound — scrypt with a salted verifier and timingSafeEqual, real RBAC/ABAC rules that read the enrolment attributes, and a token implementation that matches presented claims against issued claims rather than trusting the caller.

F1 traced all 16 Phase 0/1/5 exit-criteria rows and the Phase 1/5 work items against the frozen snapshot. Six criteria are genuinely proven by a named executable check; six are implemented but their register evidence is wrong, partial or too weak; three are honestly owner-blocked; one (P1-4) is mislabelled. Two blockers: the shipped evidence chain is self-contradictory (a PASS attestation binds a report that is red on disk, digest mismatch), and the PWA renders the dark theme by default, contradicting the recorded P1-4 met and Accepted ADR-0011. The recurring defect class is evidence that proves a different behaviour than the criterion text: P1-1 cites a test file with no enrolment test, P0-4 cites a file with no tokens, P5-4 cites a test that skips half the criterion, and P0-2/P0-5 cite checks that cannot fail on the exact defect. Eleven of sixteen ADR owner rows contradict the ADR prose, and ADR-0013 records a repository/node:sqlite seam that does not exist. Every gap found is closable in code; none requires an owner decision.

The OneKey package is a real, thoughtfully commented implementation - the fallback chain, the typed error taxonomy, the attempt trail and the policy hard rules are genuinely there - but several load-bearing promises are only prose. PROVEN by execution against a copy of the snapshot: the egress boundary has zero production callers and the one network adapter ships raw grounded context (safeguarding/disability notes) to the provider; a live provider empty answer reaches the learner as an empty lesson; a zero-usage answer throws an untyped Error out of the learner path; the Tier 0 last-resort serves an unrelated lesson while claiming it covers this topic; and the policy engine routes on the CLIENT-declared data class, ignoring the server-side policy. The credit-exhaustion guarantee is real only when a caller wires a Tier 0 provider, the hard cap does not bound real provider spend, the kill switch and circuit breaker are per-process, and the failover drill [0,1,2,3,4] report is a Set union over three different requests that hides tier 0 being visited twice and skipped once. Nothing outside apps/cli/src/selftest.ts consumes the package, so no learner-facing application exists yet to expose or mask these paths.

packages/ledger implements an in-memory hash-chained event log with deterministic hashing, PII name/value guards, private-store redaction, 60% reinvestment math, and sponsor aggregation, but not a durable SQLite-backed ledger. Core integrity controls are partial: append-only is API-level only (mutable `all()` exposure), verification is opt-in, and there is no persistence, WAL, or concurrency serialization. Money handling is mostly integer-safe in computations/reads yet append accepts negative money-key values and sponsor metrics silently default on key drift. No-PII and 60% claims are bounded by implementation semantics (pattern-based PII scan, timestamp-window attribution, no semantic dedupe) rather than absolute guarantees.
